edges.description: Failed joint separation produces proximal interphalangeal synostosis.
Abnormal cavitation and ossification extend to carpal and tarsal joints.
Abnormal skeletal joint separation can include humeroradial fusion.
Abnormal joint morphogenesis can involve cervical spine joint fusion.
Progressive synostosis limits joint range of motion and produces stiffness.
Middle-ear ossicular fixation in the synostosis spectrum produces conductive hearing impairment.
Altered BMP signaling in limb development contributes to shortened digits.
Altered BMP signaling in limb development contributes to broad thumbs.

nodes.description: Normal joint formation requires interzone specification and subsequent cavitation. Both routes above disrupt this process: excess BMP signaling from loss of noggin antagonism (SYNS1) or from noggin-resistant GDF5/GDF6 ligands (SYNS2, SYNS4), and loss of FGF9 receptor signaling at the prospective joint (SYNS3). Either way joint space formation fails and synostosis is progressive.

nodes.description: NOG mutations reduce noggin's ability to antagonize BMPs (particularly BMP2, BMP4, and GDF5), leading to excessive BMP signaling in developing joints. This causes progressive ossification and fusion of joints that would normally remain separate. GDF5 mutations cause gain-of-function changes that similarly enhance BMP pathway activity in joint development, and the SYNS4 GDF6 p.Y444N variant raises BMP signaling by the same route, resisting noggin-mediated antagonism.

nodes.description: SYNS3 is caused by the FGF9 p.S99N substitution, which is secreted normally but binds FGFR poorly, so FGF signaling in the developing joint is reduced rather than increased. FGF9 normally restrains mesenchymal cells from differentiating into chondrocytes at the prospective joint site and sustains Gdf5 expression there; the mutant protein does neither, and the interzone fails to form. This is a separate route to the same synostoses from the BMP-side lesions in SYNS1, SYNS2 and SYNS4, and it converges on the same failure of joint separation.

evidence.reference_title: Multiple synostoses syndrome is due to a missense mutation in exon 2 of FGF9 gene.
evidence.snippet: Importantly, the binding of FGF9(S99N) to its receptor is severely impaired although the dimerization ability of mutant FGF9 itself or with wild-type FGF9 is not detectably affected, providing a basis for the defective FGFR signaling.

evidence.reference_title: A point mutation in Fgf9 impedes joint interzone formation leading to multiple synostoses syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Further study reveals that the S99N mutation in Fgf9 disrupts joint interzone formation by affecting the chondrogenic differentiation of mesenchymal cells at the early stage of joint development.
